1.pericope_label: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord

schools.summary: Augustine makes the blessedness conditional, since all desire bliss and all fear the purity through which alone it comes, and observes that the workers of wickedness search these same testimonies because they prefer being learned to being righteous.

Calvin finds the psalm difficult to epitomise, since the writer passes from topic to topic and prosecutes none continuously, though exhortation to godliness and the rule of true worship run through it; Gill refers the sinlessness of the third verse to the new creature rather than to freedom from indwelling sin.

Spurgeon denies that the repetitions are tautology and traces the changes rung on three words through the eight verses, and describes devotion gleaming through them like sunlight through an olive grove; Henry runs a school metaphor through his notes, that we remain scholars in Christ’s school for life but should aim to be head-scholars, and warns that religion must be the rule of our walk and not merely the subject of our discourse.

Clarke sets out the acrostic scheme and concludes that all connection is sacrificed to it, lists the ten words by which the revelation is named and reports the claim that one of them stands in every verse but one, insists that no command was given which God knew to be impossible, and warns that allowing one commandment to be transgressed soon sets aside the whole ten; Wesley defines respect as allowing oneself in no known sin and neglecting no known duty.

Ellicott renders the sixth verse as looking into a mirror, the law showing a man his defects so that the faithful have no cause to blush, and cites a heathen moralist as bearing witness to the same rule of one way; Keil and Delitzsch set out the arithmetic of the acrostic and collect the names given the psalm by the old authorities, ending with the inscription it carries in their own tongue.

debates: Has this psalm any order of thought? Clarke holds that all connection is sacrificed to the artificial arrangement; the paragraph attached to Calvin’s block reports that a profound religious philosopher inclined the same way, describing the psalm as manifold reflections and sprightly ejaculations not ranged in any strict order but like a variety of wholesome herbs, and then answers him, objecting that it has been too commonly assumed to be a collection of unconnected thoughts; Spurgeon takes the same side against Clarke, denying tautology and tracing the changes rung on three words through the stanza; Calvin himself says only that no subject is prosecuted continuously.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch collect the names given this psalm by the old authorities, including the Talmudic remark that it consists of eight Alephs, and end with the inscription it bears in their own language, the Christian’s golden alphabet of the praise, love, power and use of the word of God.
Clarke reports the almost universal claim that one of the ten names for the revelation stands in every verse of the psalm except a single one, and says closer inspection modifies it.
Ellicott quotes a Latin treatise on friendship to show that even heathen ethics bore witness to there being one way from which a man must not turn aside.
Henry observes that though Christ keeps a free school and teaches without money, he expects his scholars to give him thanks.
themes: blessedness offered on a condition men fear
an alphabet imposed on the matter of the psalm
order in the psalm asserted and denied
the law as a mirror rather than a burden
obedience required entire or lost altogether

9.pericope_label: Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? thy word have I hid in mine heart

schools.summary: Spurgeon analyses the difficulty in two directions, the way needing to be cleansed of sins already committed and kept clear of those temptation will set before it; Henry widens the question to how the next generation may be made better, observes that few young people ask it for themselves, holds the word will do more than the laws of princes or the morals of philosophers, and says there is no laying up a treasure safely but in the heart, since houses may be robbed and memories fail.

Gill takes the hidden word as a choice treasure laid up in mind and memory for future use, reads the declaring of the judgments as the revealed will rather than the acts of providence, and finds the way of the testimonies to be Christ himself.

Clarke draws a rut or cart-track out of the word for way, and runs a single numbered programme of fifteen particulars straight through the eight verses, from considering one’s way impure to never forgetting what God has done, promising that whoever attends to them will have his way cleansed; Wesley universalises the subject, holding that any man is meant and the young man named only for his inexperience.

Ellicott would render the question as asking by what means a young man may purify his way so as to keep it according to God’s word, holds that no direct answer is given and that the omission strengthens rather than impairs the impression, finds the self-mistrust of the tenth verse a proof of the first clause, and denies that the mention of youth dates the psalm to that period of life; Keil and Delitzsch state the stanza’s argument as walking blamelessly by acting in accordance with the word.

debates: Is the question of the ninth verse answered? Henry, Spurgeon, Clarke and Wesley all take the second clause as the answer, that the way is cleansed by heeding it according to God’s word; Ellicott renders the clause instead as the standard to be reached rather than the means to be used, and holds that no direct answer is given anywhere, the reply being left to be inferred from the whole psalm, that men can do nothing of themselves — adding that the omission strengthens rather than impairs the impression on the reader.
outliers: Clarke runs one numbered list of fifteen particulars continuously through all eight verses of the stanza, from considering that one’s way is impure to forgetting neither what God has done nor what one has promised, and closes by undertaking that any young man who attends to them will have his impure way cleansed.

Ellicott denies that the mention of a young man dates the psalm to youth, and suggests instead a writer looking back on youth from old age, as in a poem of his own century, with satisfaction that even then he aimed at the best he knew.
Henry holds that a treasure kept in houses and hands may be taken by enemies and one kept only in the head may be lost by failing memory, so that the heart is the only safe place for it.
Clarke says the verb of the sixteenth verse is very emphatic and means to skip about and jump for joy.
themes: a question asked on behalf of those who do not ask it
an answer withheld and inferred from the whole
purity needed both behind and ahead
a fifteen-point programme laid over eight verses
the word stored where it cannot be stolen or forgotten

17.pericope_label: Deal bountifully with thy servant: open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law

schools.summary: Spurgeon reads the stanzas as successive characters, the youth of the last giving way here to a servant and pilgrim in an enemy’s country, and notes that asking bounty rather than reward shuts out any legal claim; Henry makes life a mercy chiefly as an opportunity of obedience, gets the force of the stranger from the speaker’s high station, and observes that hard and foul words break no bones yet are grievous to a tender spirit.

Gill holds that the veil of ignorance must be removed before spiritual things can be discerned, distinguishes being a stranger to the world from being a stranger to divine things, and canvasses three candidates for the proud, the fallen angels, the teachers rebuked in the Gospels, and profane persons generally.

Clarke finds the stanza opening with a word from which its own governing letter is named and calls this a stroke of art, remarks that the scriptures are plain enough and that the Bible needs a comment less than the soul needs the light of the Spirit, reads the stranger historically of wandering or of captives still feeling themselves in exile, and reports manuscripts reading strangers or the heathen for the proud; Wesley makes the stranger a pilgrim travelling homeward.

Ellicott holds the stranger to describe the general transitory condition of life rather than any circumstance of the writer’s history, gives five ancient renderings of the rare verb for the soul breaking and concludes that they point to a different reading or sense than the lexicons allow, and prefers the older division of the twenty-first verse that makes the curse a separate clause; Keil and Delitzsch state the stanza’s aim as a life’s purpose held under fear of apostasy and under persecution.

debates: In what sense is the speaker a stranger in the earth? Ellicott holds that the general transitory condition of human life is meant and not any particular circumstance of the writer’s history, the mortal lacking both time and strength for the knowledge God alone teaches; Clarke reads it historically, of a man obliged to wander from place to place and so a stranger in his own country, or of captives who after seventy years still felt themselves in exile; Henry finds the force in the speaker’s station, a man who knew the world as well as most and still called himself a stranger.

What does the rare verb of the twentieth verse mean? Ellicott reports that it occurs in only one other place and lists five ancient renderings, greatly desired, was perfect, had confidence and longed among them, concluding that they point either to a different reading or to a different sense from the one the lexicons give; Clarke consults no version but English usage instead, since we say a thing broke the heart, and takes the phrase for excessive longing and hopeless love.
outliers: Clarke observes that the verb opening this stanza is the root of the name of the letter that heads all eight of its verses, so that the section begins by naming its own initial, and calls this a stroke of the psalmist’s ingenuity.
Clarke remarks that the scriptures are plain enough and the heart of man darkened by sin, so that the Bible does not so much need a comment as the soul needs the light of the Holy Spirit.
Spurgeon notes that asking for bounty rather than reward shuts out the idea of a legal claim, the wages sought being measured by God’s goodness rather than by the asker’s merit.
themes: a stanza that opens by naming its own letter
sight treated as the thing lacking rather than light
pilgrimage read as a condition and as a history
a rare verb the versions could not agree on
pride found at the bottom of every wilful sin

25.pericope_label: My soul cleaveth unto the dust: quicken thou me according to thy word

schools.summary: Spurgeon gathers the dust into three senses at once, the mourner’s ashes glued to him, the death-dust half choking him, and an earthly-mindedness he bemoans, and plays the English letter of the stanza against the Hebrew, finding depression sung in the spirit of devotion, determination and dependence; Henry offers corruption or affliction for the same figure, says the speaker was conscious of a proneness to lying and names two occasions of it, and holds the choosing Christian likely to be the steady one.

Gill has the soul melting like wax before the fire, denies that the speaker was addicted to lying to men, and reads the way of lying as false doctrine, false worship, error, superstition and idolatry, taking the chosen way of truth as Christ himself.

Clarke would render the noun as life and take the dust for an apprehension of approaching death, derives the verb of the twenty-eighth verse from distilling or dropping as tears, and notices that the word for sticking to the testimonies is the same as the word for cleaving to the dust; Wesley reads the opening as danger of present death and asks for an accurate knowledge of the word to govern himself by.

Ellicott allows summer dust as a type of despondency but prefers the dust of death, reports that the older versions render the melting verb as slumbered and holds this to suit better with the following clause, cites two modern poets and an emperor doing public penance on this verse, reads the way of lying as insincerity toward God rather than falsehood to men, and takes the reiterated prayer for quickening as a nation’s petition for revived covenant glory; Keil and Delitzsch read the dust socially, of a man held down by proscription and unable to raise himself.

debates: What holds the soul to the dust? Clarke and Wesley read an apprehension of approaching death; Ellicott prefers the dust of death while allowing summer dryness as a type of despondency; Henry offers either corruption or affliction; Keil and Delitzsch read it socially, of proscription and non-recognition; Spurgeon takes the mourner’s ashes, the death-dust and earthly-mindedness together.

What is the way of lying? Henry takes it of plain untruth and holds the speaker conscious of a proneness to it, naming two recorded occasions on which he deceived men under pressure; Gill denies he was addicted to that sin at all and reads the phrase as a false way, meaning false doctrine, false worship, error and idolatry; Ellicott makes it insincerity and unfaithfulness toward God rather than falsehood to men.

Does the soul melt or slumber in the twenty-eighth verse? Gill and Clarke keep melting, from a verb meaning to drop or distil like tears; Ellicott reports the older versions rendering it slumbered and holds that reading to suit far better with the next clause, which literally asks God to make him rise up.
outliers: Ellicott records that an emperor recited this stanza’s first verse while doing public penance at a cathedral door for a massacre.
Spurgeon observes that this portion has D for its alphabetical letter and sings of depression in the spirit of devotion, determination and dependence.

Henry compares laying the judgments before oneself to a learner setting his copy before him or a workman his model, and holds that the choosing Christian is likely to be the steady one while those who are Christians by chance tack about if the wind turn.
Clarke notes that the word used for sticking to the testimonies is the same as the word for the soul cleaving to the dust, so that the second clinging answers the first.
themes: dust read as death, as grief, as corruption and as disgrace
a stanza letter answered in the language of the reader
a melting soul that the versions made a sleeping one
deliberate choice preferred to inherited habit
a petition read against the petitioner’s own record

33.pericope_label: Teach me, O Lord, the way of thy statutes: turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity

schools.summary: Henry marks the stanza’s order, the earlier prayer having asked for an enlightened understanding and this one for a bowed will, holds an unsanctified understanding no better than none, works the danger of the eye as a physics of attention in which a gazing traveller gets over no ground, and ends with the rule that what God has promised we must pray for, being neither so aspiring as to ask more nor so modest as to ask less.

Gill grants the law cannot be kept perfectly by any mere man but holds it may be kept spiritually from love and gratitude, and reports two Jewish commentators referring the feared reproach to the speaker’s own recorded sins in a notorious case.

Clarke holds that understanding the spiritual reference of the statutes required a teaching only God could give, warns against the eye with a four-verb chain about a man who saw, coveted, took, hid his theft and was slain, and quotes an unattributed note reading the feared reproach as a private confession of a secret evil; Wesley explains why covetousness is singled out, as most opposite to the testimonies, most common a hindrance, and most pernicious as the root of all evil.

Ellicott notes that the adverb rendered to the end is peculiar to this psalm, derives the word for path from a root meaning to tread so that it is the way plain with the tracks of past pilgrims, renders the covetousness as rapine or prey, suspects idols behind the vanity, calls the received explanation of the thirty-eighth verse improbable and offers two others, and prefers to read the feared reproach as one suffered from men for obedience; Keil and Delitzsch make the stanza a prayer for guidance out of the by-paths of selfishness and disavowal.

debates: What reproach is feared in the thirty-ninth verse? Gill reports Jarchi and Kimchi referring it to the speaker’s own recorded sins, and Henry says he was conscious of having given occasion to blaspheme; Clarke offers first the reproach a godly life attracts, since such a life was never fashionable in any time or country, and then quotes an unattributed note reading the verse as a private confession of a secret evil that its author begs may never meet the eye of man; Ellicott allows the disgrace of disobedience but prefers, from the following verse, a reproach suffered from men for keeping the law.

What does the phrase about being devoted to thy fear mean? Ellicott calls the usual explanation of the elliptical expression improbable and offers instead that the word establishes fear, or more likely that the promise established belongs to those who fear God; Henry builds his whole account of the good man on the rendering Ellicott discards.
outliers: Clarke quotes an unattributed note he had found on the thirty-ninth verse, reading it as the prayer of a man who has done a secret evil and begs that it never become public.
Clarke warns against the eye with a chain of four verbs, of a man who saw, coveted, took, hid his theft and was slain for his sin.
Ellicott derives the word for path from a root meaning to tread, so that it is the trodden way, plain with the track of all the pious feet of past times.
Henry observes that a traveller who stands gazing at every object in view will not get over ground.
themes: knowledge asked first and then the will to use it
the eye treated as the road into the heart
covetousness singled out as the root hindrance
a feared reproach read as guilt and as fidelity
a promise made the exact measure of a prayer

41.pericope_label: Let thy mercies come also unto me, O Lord: I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings

schools.summary: Spurgeon notes that the request for mercy is plural because the need was much and varied, and that mercy was asked as well as teaching since the man was guilty as well as ignorant; Henry makes liberty a paradox, the service of sin being perfect slavery and the service of God perfect liberty, so that licentiousness is bondage to the greatest of tyrants and conscientiousness freedom to the meanest of prisoners.

Gill supplies the taunt that there is no help for the speaker in God, guards the broad way of the forty-fifth verse against the broad road that leads to destruction by making it the law that is exceeding broad, names the courts before which the speaker had spoken in his youth and in his reign, and takes the lifted hands for esteem, prayer, an oath and the setting of the hand to work.

Clarke reads the liberty as release from a present political bondage, rejects a scholar’s attempt to refer the speaking before kings to a foreign king the psalmist had instructed, referring it instead to those who spoke courageously before the kings of the exile, and turns the verse about loving the commandments into a rebuke of Christians who feel less for the Gospel than a Jew felt for ordinances affording far smaller privileges; Wesley reads the lifted hands as receiving and embracing.

Ellicott renders the answer to the reviler literally as answering him a word, so that pronouncing God’s promise is itself the reply, and supports this from the repetition of the same noun in the next verse; he renders liberty as a large place, supplies the ellipsis of the lifted hands as prayer for power to obey, and records that the old Latin of the verse about kings became the motto of a famous confession of faith. Keil and Delitzsch secure the plural of the opening word against the Greek and read the stanza as a prayer for fearless confession.

debates: Before which kings does the speaker undertake to talk of the testimonies? Gill names the courts of the speaker’s own youth and the kings who later visited his reign, and Henry that kings were sometimes his judges before he came to the crown; Clarke reports a scholar referring the verse to a particular foreign king whom the psalmist had instructed in his religion, rejects that because he holds the psalm compiled during the captivity, and refers the words instead to those who spoke courageously before the kings of the exile.
outliers: Ellicott records that the old Latin of the verse about speaking before kings, following the Greek in its tenses, was taken as the motto of a famous confession of faith.

Clarke turns the verse about loving the commandments into a rebuke of his own readers, that it shames Christians to feel so little affection for the Gospel when such inviolate attachment appears here in a Jew toward ordinances that afforded not a thousandth part of the privileges.
Ellicott reads the answer given to a reviler as being itself a word, so that pronouncing the promise is the whole of the reply.
Spurgeon observes that he who said let there be light can also say let there be mercy.
themes: mercy asked in the plural for a varied need
a promise recited as the answer to a taunt
obedience described as room rather than restraint
testimony undertaken in the presence of power
hands lifted in esteem, oath, prayer and work

49.pericope_label: Remember the word unto thy servant: thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage

schools.summary: Spurgeon notices that the plea asks God to remember his own word rather than the speaker’s service, and observes wryly that servants do not usually wish their masters to remember what was said to them; Henry lists the jeers made against piety as cant, mopishness and needless preciseness, answers that a traveller goes on though the dogs bark, locates the horror in contempt shown to God rather than in danger to himself, and ends with the maxim that God’s work is its own wages.

Gill divides the judgments remembered into those executed on the wicked and those dealt providentially to God’s own people, canvasses four senses of the house of pilgrimage and prefers the whole course of life, supporting it from two ancient philosophers who called this life a kind of pilgrimage, and reads the derided speaker as a type of one later derided by the same class of scorners.

Clarke reads the remembered promise, the comfort and the songs alike of release from captivity, and identifies the word for horror with the pestilential burning wind of the Arabs, taking it for horror at sin as something corrupting and mortal; Wesley makes the horror a mixed passion of abhorrence, dread and sorrow, and the remembered judgments strictly punitive.

Ellicott notes that the noun for comfort occurs in only one other place and would repunctuate the line so that the comfort is the quickening itself, names the same desert wind as Clarke but renders the word violent indignation rather than horror, and weighs a reference to the exile in the house of pilgrimage before preferring the transitoriness of human life, rendering the statutes as music in the house of his sojournings; Keil and Delitzsch likewise have the speaker burning with indignation at the apostates.

debates: Is the fifty-third verse horror or indignation? Clarke identifies the word with the pestilential burning wind of the Arabs and takes it for horror at the destructive nature of sin; Ellicott names the same wind but renders the word violent indignation, a storm of rage, and Keil and Delitzsch agree, describing the speaker as burning with indignation at the apostates; Wesley calls it a mixed passion of abhorrence, dread and sorrow; Henry does not name the feeling but fixes its cause in the contempt shown to God rather than in any danger to the speaker.

What is the house of pilgrimage? Gill offers a fugitive’s unsettled state, a palace regarded as an inn, the body as a tabernacle, or the whole course of life, preferring the last; Clarke reads it of the captivity; Ellicott weighs that reference and sets it aside for the transitoriness of human life.
outliers: Gill supports the reading of life as a pilgrimage from two ancient philosophers who used the same figure.

Henry lists the jeers made against piety, that praying was called cant, seriousness mopishness and strictness needless preciseness, and answers that a traveller goes on his way though the dogs bark at him.
Spurgeon observes that the words of masters to servants are not usually such that servants wish them remembered, since they record the faults of work that did not answer the command.
Henry closes the stanza with the maxim that God’s work is its own wages, a heart to obey being itself the reward of obedience.
themes: a promise pleaded rather than a service
mockery answered by not so much as declining
one word read as terror and as fury
life described as lodging on a journey
statutes turned into travelling songs

57.pericope_label: Thou art my portion, O Lord: at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee

schools.summary: Spurgeon holds the opening sentence better left broken as an exclamation, my portion, O Lord, and has the poet seizing his share as of a divided spoil; Henry builds the character of a godly man on the received reading, reaches the embroidery figure independently for the thinking on one’s ways, observes that what we do follows us where what we have cannot, notes the reverence of rising in the cold and the dark, and remarks that public worship will not excuse us from secret worship.

Gill follows the received sense of being robbed and supplies three occasions of plunder from the speaker’s history while reporting a Jewish commentator who rejects that sense for taking hold of, and recalls two prisoners who sang praises at the same midnight hour.

Clarke treats the psalm as selected diary notes whose order was distorted to serve the acrostic, and renumbers this stanza into seven steps in the order of grace rather than of the text, ending at the portion where the text begins; he renders the verb for delaying as standing what-what-whating, and takes the thinking on one’s ways for a metaphor from embroidery in which the cloth is turned at every stitch; Wesley reads the injuries as suffered for respect to the law.

Ellicott would mend the broken opening so that the portion is not God himself but the keeping of his words, and reports that all the ancient versions but one make the cords of the wicked surround rather than rob the speaker; Keil and Delitzsch likewise make the portion the understanding and keeping of the word, the highest favour that can come to a man.

debates: What is the portion claimed in the opening verse? Spurgeon would leave the broken sentence bare as an exclamation and takes God himself for the portion, as Henry does in building the character of a godly man upon it; Ellicott mends the ellipsis differently and makes the portion the keeping of God’s words rather than God, and Keil and Delitzsch agree, calling the understanding and keeping of the word the highest favour a man can receive.

Did the wicked rob the speaker or surround him? Gill follows the received sense and names three occasions of plunder from the speaker’s history, while reporting a Jewish commentator who rejects that sense of the word for taking hold of; Ellicott says all the ancient versions but one make the cords of the wicked surround him; Clarke keeps the cords as snares and has the wicked hunting like wild beasts.
outliers: Clarke treats the whole psalm as notes selected from diaries formed at different times, holds that the acrostic forced the author to put behind what in the order of grace comes before, and accordingly renumbers this stanza into seven steps of his own arrangement.
Clarke renders the verb for not delaying as not standing what-what-whating, or shilly-shallying with oneself.
Clarke and Henry independently take the thinking on one’s ways for a metaphor from embroidery, where the figure must show the same on both sides and the cloth is turned at every stitch.

Henry notes that the man rose from his bed at midnight, perhaps in the cold and the dark, to make the thanksgiving more solemn, and was a good husband of time in rising to pray when he could not sleep.
themes: a broken sentence mended two opposite ways
a psalm re-ordered against its own alphabet
self-examination compared to turning embroidery
plunder or encirclement in a single verb
worship kept up where no one could see it

65.pericope_label: Thou hast dealt well with thy servant: it is good for me that I have been afflicted

schools.summary: Spurgeon treats the whole stanza as a sermon on its own first verse; Henry renders the thing asked for as a good relish by which things that differ are discerned, blames prosperity for making men conceited, indulgent and deaf to reproof, and ends with the son whose distress brought him first to himself and then to his father.

Gill expands the good taste of the sixty-sixth verse into a spiritual discernment that distinguishes truth from error, acquits the speaker of anything wilful in his straying by making it weakness and negligence rather than contempt, renders the forged lie as one sewn on or stitched to another, and compares the fat heart to creatures grown too fat for feeling.

Clarke renders the request as a good taste and discernment, compresses the doctrine of the stanza into the epigram that affliction sanctified is a great blessing and unsanctified an additional curse, and refers the forged lie to captives whose motives were continually misrepresented; Wesley reads the fat heart as stupidity and insensibility.

Ellicott renders the request as good taste in a moral rather than an artistic sense and suggests tact or delicate moral perception, observes that the higher this psalm’s conception of God rises the more earnest its prayer for guidance in conduct becomes, holds beyond much doubt that the exile is alluded to in the sixty-seventh verse, and renders the forged lie as patched, comparing Greek and Latin idioms for stitching deceit and a line from a play; Keil and Delitzsch make the good word of God the fountain of all good, learned in the way of lowliness.

debates: What is asked for in the sixty-sixth verse? Henry, Clarke, Gill and Ellicott all agree that the word means taste rather than judgment, Henry calling it a good relish by which things that differ are discerned, Gill making it the palate that detects what is perverse in food, and Ellicott specifying a moral rather than an artistic sense and suggesting tact or delicate moral perception; Wesley alone keeps the received rendering and adds an experimental knowledge to it.
outliers: Ellicott renders the forged lie as patched and compares a Greek and a Latin idiom for stitching deceit, together with a line from a play in which one character accuses another of patching up his excuses; Gill independently renders the same verb as sewing a lie on or stitching one lie to another.
Clarke reduces the doctrine of the stanza to the epigram that affliction sanctified is a great blessing while affliction unsanctified is an additional curse.

Ellicott observes that it is characteristic of this psalm that the higher its conception of the divine nature rises, the more earnest its prayer becomes for knowledge of God’s will in matters of conduct.
Henry warns that prosperity makes people conceited of themselves, indulgent of the flesh, forgetful of God, in love with the world and deaf to the reproofs of the word.
themes: discernment asked for as a sense rather than a science
prosperity treated as the more dangerous condition
affliction credited with the recovery of obedience
slander described as a thing stitched together
insensibility figured as an over-fed heart

73.pericope_label: Thy hands have made me and fashioned me: I know, O Lord, that thy judgments are right

schools.summary: Spurgeon jokes that though every verse begins with the smallest letter the section does not treat of jots and titles, and finds a double thoughtfulness in the making and the moulding; Henry holds every man as truly God’s handiwork as the first man, marks how much harder it is to own the justice of affliction in one’s own case than in general, and reaches independently the reading that those who feared God grew strange to the speaker after his great sin.

Gill softens the corrections of the seventy-fifth verse into things done with moderation and gentleness, gives the shaming of the proud three possible ends, and says plainly that some good men had left the speaker for his enemies, reporting two Jewish commentators who referred this to the aftermath of the affair with another man’s wife.

Clarke divides the two verbs into forming the mass and giving the distinguishing form, turns the fact of creation into a request to be shown that he was made for heaven and not for earth, and reads the turning of the God-fearers as their acknowledging him a brand plucked from the burning; Wesley makes the afflictions pursuant to the promises and directed to the sufferer’s good.

Ellicott glosses the second verb as fixed or established, renders the dealing perversely of the seventy-eighth verse as bending or wronging, and finds in the seventy-fourth verse the latent truth of spiritual communion, observing that its plainer sense has been amply confirmed by history; Keil and Delitzsch argue from creation to instruction, that God cannot forsake his own creature or deny him the one thing that makes him truly happy.

debates: Why are those who fear God asked to turn to the speaker? Gill says plainly that some good men had left him and taken his enemies’ part, and reports Jarchi and Kimchi referring this to the period after his sin with another man’s wife, when those who feared the Lord would not keep his company; Henry arrives independently at the same reading, that after that foul sin they grew strange to him though he was a king; Clarke takes the verse the other way, as men seeing God’s work in him and owning him a brand plucked from the burning.
outliers: Spurgeon jokes that although every verse of this section begins with the smallest letter of the alphabet, it certainly does not treat of jots and titles and other trifles.

Henry observes that it is easier to own in general that God’s judgments are right than to own it when the case is one’s own, and that the speaker subscribes to it with application, calling even his own afflictions just and kind.
Clarke turns the fact of having been made into a request, that having been raised above the beasts he may be taught he was made for heaven and not for earth.
themes: creation urged as a reason for further making
justice of affliction owned in the first person
shame asked for as repentance or as ruin
a congregation that had drawn away from its king
deliverance of one made a comfort to many

81.pericope_label: My soul fainteth for thy salvation: for I am become like a bottle in the smoke

schools.summary: Spurgeon calls this octave the midnight of the psalm, dark and black though with stars in it and a promise of dawn in its last verse; Henry draws out the shrivelled bottle into a man once ruddy and now withered and thrown by as a vessel in which there is no pleasure, and then qualifies the complaint by noting that good men when melancholy sometimes think themselves more slighted than they really are.

Gill explains that bottles in that country were made of skins, which hung in a chimney would shrivel and become good for nothing, reads the failing eyes as worn out with waiting for a promise deferred, and holds that the enemies could reach nothing of his that was laid up in heaven.

Clarke explains the eastern skin bottle parched by smoke, records that the eighty-fourth verse contains none of the ten names for the law, reports four ancient versions in which the proud recite unholy fables rather than dig pits, and asks whether the pride of the captors will not be brought down; Wesley says the sufferer’s natural moisture is dried and burnt up.

Ellicott notes that the verbs of the first two verses are one word, reads the failing of the eyes as the strain of watching a distant object rather than exhaustion, canvasses four senses of the bottle and rejects the weakest, allowing that ancient mention of mellowing wine by heat would reverse the image into the benefit of suffering and that a variant reading might make it weeping, corrects the relative of the eighty-fifth verse to refer to the men rather than the pits, and reads the question about days as a generation’s dread of passing before deliverance comes; Keil and Delitzsch note that the words for his longing and for his enemies’ design are nearly the same sound.

debates: What is the bottle in the smoke? Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Henry all take it for a skin bottle shrivelled above a fire and so for the wasting of a man by trouble; Ellicott rejects as too weak the suggestion that it means only being set aside, allows the received sense, but notes that the ancient poets mention mellowing wine by heat, which would make the image signify the benefit of the discipline of suffering, and adds that two old versions read hoar-frost for smoke and that the word for bottle can mean a cloud, so that the whole may be another expression for weeping.

What in the eighty-fifth verse is not after the law? Henry makes it the pits themselves, since the law forbids devising evil against a neighbour and holds a man answerable for the mischief a dug pit causes; Ellicott corrects the relative to refer to the proud instead, so that the diggers and not their diggings are what stands against the law.
outliers: Clarke records that the eighty-fourth verse contains none of the ten names for the law which he had said stood in every verse of the psalm but one.
Clarke reports four ancient versions, and an old English rendering agreeing with them, in which the proud recite unholy fables instead of digging pits.
Spurgeon calls this octave the midnight of the psalm, and says that hope alone keeps the soul from fainting, by using the promise as a smelling-bottle.
Henry notes that good men when drooping and melancholy sometimes think themselves more slighted than they really are.
themes: eyes failing from strain rather than from sorrow
a shrivelled vessel read as ruin and as ripening
a verse found lacking the psalm’s own key word
pits in one text and fables in another
a generation afraid of dying before the deliverance

89.pericope_label: For ever, O Lord, thy word is settled in heaven: I have seen an end of all perfection

schools.summary: Spurgeon marks the turn from the fainting of the previous section to the God who does not faint, and turns the word settled into a rebuke of those never happier than when unsettling everything; Henry divides the settling into the secret counsel and the revealed will, describes the earth holding still against everything that might move it, distinguishes saying I am thine from saying thou art mine on the authority of an older writer, and names four undone excellences from the speaker’s history.

Gill lists what nature has not altered, the motion and distance and influence of the heavenly bodies, the seasons of the moon, the place of the fixed stars and the revolutions of the planets, and the round of seedtime and harvest, and allows the last verse a present sense, that the most perfect things will have an end and that end is at hand.

Clarke would invert the ninety-first verse to read that all are God’s servants and therefore continue according to his ordinances, holds that without the consolations of religion they would long since have died of a broken heart, and turns the claim I am thine into an appeal that God save his own; Wesley keeps the heavens and earth standing simply as God appointed them.

Ellicott keeps the received order of the ninety-first verse, takes the all to mean the whole universe, and defends the arrangement because the parallelism is preserved by it and lost by the alternative; Keil and Delitzsch derive the word’s stability from its location, since having heaven as its standing-place it has the qualities of heaven and first of all a heaven-like fixity.

debates: How should the ninety-first verse be construed? Clarke would invert its clauses, reading that all are God’s servants and therefore continue this day according to his ordinances; Ellicott keeps the received order, understands the all as the whole universe, and argues that the parallelism is preserved by this arrangement and lost by the alternative.
outliers: Henry names four excellences the speaker had seen undone in his own lifetime, the strongest man overcome, the swiftest overtaken, the wisest befooled and the fairest deformed, and calls it poor perfection which one sees an end of.

Henry borrows from an older writer the distinction that the speaker does not say thou art mine, which would be the higher challenge, but I am thine, pleading God’s property in him rather than any quality of his own.
Spurgeon turns the word settled into a rebuke, since some men are never happier than when they are unsettling everything and everybody, but God’s mind is not with them.
Henry remarks that a Bible is a pleasant companion at any time if we please.
themes: a word given the properties of the place it stands in
the fixity of nature offered as evidence
possession claimed from the weaker end
four kinds of human excellence seen to fail
a command called broad rather than long

97.pericope_label: O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day

schools.summary: Spurgeon finds love and meditation working in a circle, each producing the other, and observes that familiarity with this book breeds affection where familiarity with men often breeds the reverse; Henry raises the puzzle of how a shepherd turned soldier came by such learning, and concludes that the written word is a surer guide to heaven than all the fathers, teachers and ancients of the church.

Gill declines the softened rabbinical rendering of the comparison with teachers, offering instead that the teachers meant were bad ones or that scholars do sometimes exceed their masters, and names two such pairs; he takes the third comparison of old men rather than antiquity, and notes that words may be tasted and eaten in the language of the classical writers as well as of scripture.

Clarke reports a candidate for the psalm’s authorship in the exile who outstripped the wise men of the court that held him, then two verses later treats the same claim as most literally true of David, whose compositions he almost calls a sublime Gospel, and turns the sweetness of the words into a rebuke of Christians whose privileges are superior and whose consolations are not; Wesley reduces the stanza to the rule that the practice of religion is the best way to understand it.

Ellicott explains that the rabbinical writers disliked a scholar professing wisdom above his teachers and rendered the clause as getting wisdom from them instead, which he notes suited the way their own great commentary grew; he prefers the present tense in the ninety-eighth verse and old men rather than antiquity in the hundredth; Keil and Delitzsch infer from the vocabulary that teachers and elders formed a recognisable class at the time of writing.

debates: May a scholar claim more understanding than his teachers? Ellicott reports that the rabbinical writers disliked the idea and rendered the clause as saying he got wisdom from all his teachers, and remarks that this suited the manner in which their own commentary was built up; Gill meets the same difficulty by supposing either that the teachers meant were bad ones or that a scholar may honourably exceed his master, and names two such pairs; both prefer the bolder reading of the text.

Are the ancients of the hundredth verse the old or the antique? Ellicott holds it more probable, with the older versions generally, that old men are meant; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch agree, Gill adding that a younger man may be endued with more understanding than the aged.
outliers: Clarke reports that some have thought the psalm composed by the exile who was found wiser than all the wise men of the court that held him, and then two verses later applies the same claim most literally to David.
Henry raises the question how a man who spent his youth as a shepherd and his manhood in court and camp came by so great a stock of learning.
Gill notes that speech may be spoken of as tasted and eaten in the classical writers as well as in scripture.
Spurgeon observes that with most men the more you know them the less you admire them, but that with this book familiarity breeds affection and affection seeks greater familiarity.
themes: love professed in a cry rather than an argument
wisdom claimed above enemies, teachers and elders
a claim softened by readers who found it immodest
learning traced to a source outside the schools
a taste appealed to as the test of a doctrine

105.pericope_label: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path

schools.summary: Spurgeon supplies the practice behind the lamp, that with no fixed lights in eastern towns each traveller carried his own lantern against the open sewer and the heaps in the road, and holds that the word is given to guide the feet rather than to astound the head; Henry makes the same distinction between a light for the eyes and a light for the path, takes the oath at full strength as an allegiance sworn to a sovereign, and finds three degrees of peril in the soul carried in the hand.

Gill allows the oath of the hundred and sixth verse to be rendered as already performed rather than promised, and observes that what a man carries in his hands may easily fall or be taken from him by violence, which is why the life is said to be carried there.

Clarke distinguishes a candle held in the hand from a general light shining on all God’s works, deflates the oath into a renewal of covenant, reads the freewill offerings of the mouth as the substitute accepted from captives who cannot sacrifice, supplies two classical parallels for carrying the life in the hand, and dismisses the reading of four ancient versions there as a conjectural and useless emendation; Wesley keeps the offerings as the sacrifices of prayer and praise.

Ellicott cites a modern poet’s description of duty as a light to guide, connects the verb rendered perform with one met earlier in the psalm meaning strengthen or confirm, glosses the freewill offerings as thanks and praise, and refers the soul carried in the hand to two other places where the figure means peril; Keil and Delitzsch call the word the traveller’s torch and his sun on a way that leads close past abysses.

debates: How much does the oath of the hundred and sixth verse claim? Clarke says it perhaps means no more than that the speaker had renewed his covenant with God; Henry takes it at full force and generalises it, holding it good for us to bind ourselves by solemn oath as subjects swear allegiance to a sovereign, owning ourselves liable to the curse if we do not perform; Gill notes the verb may be rendered as an act already done rather than a promise.

What are the freewill offerings of the mouth? Ellicott, Wesley and Henry take them simply for thanks and praise; Clarke gives them a setting, as the plea of men in captivity who cannot sacrifice and ask that the praises of their mouths be accepted in place of the offerings they cannot bring to an altar.
outliers: Spurgeon explains that eastern towns had no fixed lamps and every passenger carried a lantern to avoid the open sewer and the heaps in the road, which he takes for a true picture of the path through this world.

Clarke supplies two classical parallels for the phrase about carrying the life in the hand, and then dismisses the reading of four ancient versions at that place as a conjectural and useless emendation.
Spurgeon holds that the word is not sent to astound us with its brilliance but to guide us by its instruction, since the head needs illumination but the feet need direction more.
themes: light supplied for walking rather than for looking
a lantern carried because the street has none
a vow read as covenant renewal and as sworn allegiance
praise accepted where sacrifice is impossible
a life described as held in the hand that may drop it

113.pericope_label: I hate vain thoughts: but thy law do I love. Thou art my hiding place and my shield

schools.summary: Spurgeon keeps the received sense of vain thoughts and turns it against his own decade, asking what the fashion for men of thought and modern thought is but the old pride of the human heart; Henry makes conscience of thoughts because they are words to God, warns that vain ones open the door to all evil, and states the doctrine of the upholding verses in a sentence, that we stand no longer than God holds us and go no further than he carries us.

Gill reads the dismissal of the evildoers typologically as words to be spoken again at the last account, and takes the dross of the wicked for hypocrites who passed for gold and proved reprobate silver.

Clarke makes the hated thing a class of men rather than a habit of mind, hating tumultuous and violent persons and abominating mobs and troublers of the public peace, assigns the hiding place and the shield to suffering and to fighting respectively, and sees in the dross the scum swept from melting metal before casting; Wesley takes the deceit of the wicked to bring on themselves the destruction they designed for others.

Ellicott renders the hated thing as men who halt between two opinions, thinking of those inclined for political reasons toward foreign customs, derives the verb rendered trodden down from weighing or valuing and thence from the buyer’s habit of beating down a price, comparing the English cheapen, and argues from the parallelism that the wiles of the wicked are simply fruitless; Keil and Delitzsch likewise make the hated ones the inwardly divided, who try to combine faith with naturalism.

debates: What is hated in the hundred and thirteenth verse? Henry and Spurgeon keep vain thoughts and treat them as the beginnings of sin; Clarke makes the word a class of men and the statement political, hating tumultuous persons and abominating mobs and insurrections; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree on a third sense, men who halt between two opinions, Ellicott identifying them with those politically inclined toward foreign customs and Keil and Delitzsch with men combining the true worship and heathenism.

What is said of the wicked in the hundred and eighteenth verse? Wesley takes their deceitful devices to recoil on themselves; Clarke reads the clause as saying their elevation is a lie; Ellicott argues from the parallelism that their tricks are simply in vain, paraphrasing that their wiles are as fruitless as they are deceitful, and reports four rival renderings of the preceding verb, including one that has God impaling them.
outliers: Ellicott derives the verb rendered trodden down from a root meaning to weigh or value, which took a harsher sense from the buyer’s habit of beating down a price by depreciating the goods, and compares the English word cheapen, which once meant only to buy.
Spurgeon turns the verse against the fashion of his own decade for men of thought, thoughtful preachers and modern thought, holding it the old pride of the human heart under a new name.
Clarke assigns the hiding place and the shield to two different occasions, one for suffering in secret and one for being called to fight.
themes: a single noun read as thought, as riot and as compromise
shelter and armour distinguished by occasion
perseverance made entirely dependent on being held
a verb for contempt traced to the haggling of buyers
the wicked separated as dross before casting

121.pericope_label: I have done judgment and justice: it is time for thee, Lord, to work

schools.summary: Spurgeon defends the plea of innocence against the charge of self-righteousness by distinguishing the tone used before God about our shortcomings from the tone used before men who censure us wrongly, and observes that eastern rulers commonly gave neither judgment nor justice or else judgment without justice; Henry endorses the rendering that calls on men to work for the Lord, and distinguishes sinning against the commandment from sinning away the commandment.

Gill reports that the versions divide on the word for surety, one ancient translation and two Jewish commentators making it a prayer to be delighted with good things while others keep suretyship, develops the latter as the office of Christ, reports that the hundred and twenty-sixth verse may be rendered as a call on men to work for the Lord, and notes the Jewish expectation that the Messiah would come at a time of great wickedness.

Clarke breaks into exclamation at the request for suretyship, asking God to pledge himself to produce his servant safely at the judgment of the great day, and reports that neither of the first two verses of this stanza contains any of the ten names for the revelation; Wesley reads the making void of the law as an open casting off of its authority.

Ellicott supplies three parallels for the request to be gone surety, and gives a tally of the verses lacking any name for the law that cannot be reconciled with Clarke’s; he reads the irreligion of the wicked as making the law dearer to the psalmist and quotes a line of English verse about one faithful among the faithless; Keil and Delitzsch note that the two nouns of the opening verse stand in the reverse of their usual order.

debates: How many verses of this psalm lack any of its names for the law? Clarke had claimed at the outset that only one verse lacked them, then named a verse earlier in the psalm as an exception, and here reports that neither of the first two verses of this stanza contains any; Ellicott states that the hundred and twenty-second and one later verse are the only two of the kind. The two lists cannot both stand.

Who is to work in the hundred and twenty-sixth verse? Gill reports that the words may be rendered it is time to work for the Lord, an ancient version and an Aramaic paraphrase agreeing; Henry says the original will bear this and endorses it, holding that every one must in his place appear on the Lord’s side before begging God to take the work into his own hands; Clarke keeps the received sense and refers the promised deliverance to a particular captivity.
outliers: Clarke exclaims at the word for suretyship, asking God to pledge himself to produce his servant safely at the judgment of the great day.

Spurgeon distinguishes the tone in which a man deals with God about his shortcomings from the tone in which he answers the wrongful censures of men, and holds a plea of innocence justified in the second case.
Henry distinguishes sinning against the commandment, which a godly man may do, from sinning away the commandment, which is repealing God’s laws and enacting one’s own lusts.
themes: a countable claim about the psalm that two readers count differently
God asked to stand bail for his own servant
innocence pleaded before men and not before God
a call to act read as addressed to God and to men
love for a law increased by the contempt of others

129.pericope_label: Thy testimonies are wonderful: the entrance of thy words giveth light

schools.summary: Spurgeon warns that some wonder at the words of God and use them for speculation, holding that this writer obeyed the more as he wondered the more; Henry lists the majesty of the style, the purity of the matter and the harmony of the parts as the grounds of wonder, makes admiration the test of acquaintance, adds a fourth sense of the entrance as the later covenant unfolding the earlier, and says the speaker desires no better than his neighbours’ fare.

Gill takes the entrance of the words in three senses, the opening chapters of the Bible, the word entering the heart, and the exposition of scripture by its ministers, has the panting of a man out of breath or of a hungry man waiting for food, and reports three Jewish readings that turn the oppression of man inward, as the oppression of the first man, his sin, or the corruption of nature.

Clarke makes the entrance a personal act, since light springs up when he opens his Bible and every sermon and prayer is an opening by which light is let in, and reverses the panting into the flight of a hunted animal running open-mouthed for the cooling air, its strength nearly spent; Wesley glosses the wonder as deep mysteries and the panting as thirst after the precepts.

Ellicott renders the entrance literally as opening and prefers the older versions’ manifestation or declaration, rejects both the received rendering and the marginal correction of the hundred and thirty-second verse in favour of according to the right of those who love God’s name, since the mercy is theirs by covenant and not merely by custom, and notes that the cognate root of the verb for dominion gives the title sultan in a neighbouring language; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the wonderful as paradoxical, exalted above common understanding.

debates: What is the entrance of God’s words? Gill offers the opening chapters of the Bible, the word’s entry into the heart, and the exposition of scripture by ministers; Henry gives the same three and adds that some understand the later covenant as the unfolding of the earlier; Ellicott renders it literally opening and prefers manifestation or declaration with the older versions; Clarke makes it the reader’s own act of opening the book, and every sermon, prayer and act of faith an opening by which light is let in.

What is the oppression of man in the hundred and thirty-fourth verse? Henry and Clarke take it plainly of human enemies who may be reminded that they are but men; Gill reports three Jewish readings that turn it inward, as the oppression of the first man, as the sin of that man from which the Lord’s people are redeemed, or as the corruption of nature which oppresses everybody.
outliers: Clarke reads the panting as the flight of an animal exhausted in the chase, running open-mouthed for the cooling air with its strength nearly spent, so that salvation is sought as a man would run from a ferocious beast for his life.
Ellicott notes that the cognate root of the verb for having dominion appears in a neighbouring language as the title sultan.

Ellicott rejects both the received rendering and the margin at the hundred and thirty-second verse, holding that what those who love God’s name receive is theirs by right of covenant and not merely by his custom.
Henry makes admiration of the testimonies the test of acquaintance with them, holding that not to admire is a sign of not understanding.
themes: a revelation called strange as well as excellent
one noun read as beginning, entry and exposition
longing figured as a hunted animal gasping for air
custom claimed as covenant right
oppression sought outside the man and found within

137.pericope_label: Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright are thy judgments: thy word is very pure

schools.summary: Spurgeon notes that the governing letter of the section sounds like the Hebrew for righteousness so that the alphabet sets the keynote, and observes that the divine name is used rarely in so long a psalm because familiarity with God begets reverence rather than carelessness; Henry draws from the zeal of the stanza the rule that the worse others are the better we should be, and ends by binding God’s truth and God’s law together as one thing.

Gill reports a rendering that makes the small one young and refers it to the years before the anointing though he prefers condition to age, takes the purity as silver tried in a furnace and purified seven times, and makes the everlasting righteousness the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer.

Clarke turns the word for purity from passive to active, since it is purification rather than a purified thing, a fire to purify as well as a hammer to break, draws the practical consequence of being small and despised, and observes that the word for righteousness covers not only God’s perfection but his method of treating men and his plan of redemption; Wesley glosses the purity as freedom from the least mixture of falsehood.

Ellicott refers the opening verse to a historian’s account of an emperor who died reciting it, moves the verb commandest back across the verse boundary to obtain what he calls the simple and obvious sense, renders the purity as purged by trial so that the proved excellence of the word is what is loved, and denies that the words about being small and despised are applicable to an individual at all, referring them to a small nation among great powers; Keil and Delitzsch keep young for small and note a point of word order.

debates: Who is small and despised? Gill reports a rendering that makes the word young and refers it to the years before the speaker’s anointing, though he prefers to take it of condition; Keil and Delitzsch keep young; Henry makes it a portrait of a man both pious and poor whose very excellency exposed him to contempt; Clarke draws the practical consequence that being small he cannot resist and being despised he is in danger; Ellicott alone holds the words hardly applicable to an individual and refers them to a small nation standing among the great powers of the east.

Is the word pure or purifying? Clarke makes the term active, purification rather than a purified thing, a fire to purify as well as a hammer to break; Ellicott and Gill keep it passive, Ellicott rendering it purged by trial and noting that the older versions have fired, so that the proved excellence of the word is the ground of love for it.
outliers: Ellicott sends the reader to a historian’s account of an emperor who died with the opening words of this stanza on his lips.
Ellicott moves the verb of the second verse back into the first to obtain what he calls the simple and obvious sense, and asserts that another arrangement of the text is unquestionably correct.
Spurgeon observes that the initial letter of every verse here sounds like the Hebrew word for righteousness, so that the alphabet supplies the keynote.
Spurgeon notes that the divine name occurs rarely in so vast a psalm, because those most familiar with God use it least carelessly.
themes: a theme announced by the sound of a letter
a verse division questioned in an acrostic poem
purity claimed as an effect rather than a quality
smallness read as youth, as poverty and as a nation
law and truth identified with each other

145.pericope_label: I cried with my whole heart: I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried

schools.summary: Spurgeon lays the stanza out as eight answers, one to a verse, insists that a prayer without elocution or doctrine will reach God if the whole heart is in it, and gives the maxim that he who has been with God in the closet will find God with him in the furnace; Henry warns that lip-labour is lost labour, praises the speaker as an early riser who was none of those saying yet a little sleep, and notes that God brings us into perils so that we may wrestle for a blessing.

Gill has the pursuers drawing near like huntsmen after their sport so that the speaker’s life drew nigh to his destroyers, and grades the nearness of God into four kinds, of relation, of union, of communion and of gracious presence.

Clarke promises that whoever cries with his whole heart will not leave the throne of grace without a blessing, renders the verb as going before the dawn, supplies the division of the night into three watches of four hours and afterwards into four of three, has the psalmist rising at each proclamation of a watch, and states the antithesis of the close in a line, that as they are near to destroy so God is near to save; Wesley takes the plea of the hundred and forty-ninth verse simply as the word.

Ellicott notes that the word rendered dawning means literally breath and is used of the fresh breeze at sunset as well as at sunrise, so that the verse does not itself say which twilight is meant, and holds that the noun of the hundred and forty-ninth verse must bear the sense of custom, citing with approval the old liturgical rendering according as thou art wont; Keil and Delitzsch take the morning twilight while denying that the verb means anticipating it.

debates: Which twilight does the hundred and forty-seventh verse name? Ellicott observes that the Hebrew means literally breath and is used of the fresh breeze blowing at sunset as well as at sunrise, being generally rendered twilight, so that the verse does not of itself decide; Clarke keeps the received sense of going before the dawn, and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the morning is meant while disputing that the verb means to anticipate it.

What is pleaded in the hundred and forty-ninth verse? Henry takes the word for God’s wisdom, since he knows what we need, or else for his promise; Wesley makes it simply the word; Ellicott holds that the noun must here bear the sense of a custom, and cites with approval the old liturgical rendering, according as thou art wont.
outliers: Clarke supplies the timekeeping of the night watches, three of four hours each beginning at six in the evening until the Romans taught a division into four of three hours, and holds that the psalmist rose at the proclaiming of each watch; he promises a remarkable custom of our own ancestors when he reaches a later verse of this psalm.
Spurgeon holds that a prayer without beauty of elocution, length of expression, depth of doctrine or accuracy of diction will still find its way to the heart of God if the whole heart is in it.
Gill grades the nearness of God into four kinds, of relation, of union, of communion and of gracious presence.
themes: a stanza read as eight answers to eight questions
prayer measured by the heart rather than the phrasing
devotion timed by the watchman’s call
one word that will serve for either twilight
pursuers near and a deliverer nearer

153.pericope_label: Consider mine affliction, and deliver me: great are thy tender mercies, O Lord

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the opening verb the key-word of the stanza and notes that it asks for consideration rather than haste, calling the words for the affliction picturesque as portioning off a special spot of woe for the writer alone; Henry marks that the plea is to consider how the speaker loves the precepts and not how he fulfils them, makes the distance of salvation from the wicked a moving one, and cites a maxim of the civil law to show that God’s word did not gain validity by lapse of time.

Gill distinguishes several distances at which salvation stands from the wicked, its author, its word, an experimental knowledge of it and its enjoyment in heaven, keeps sorrow rather than loathing at the transgressors while noting that the noun means the treacherous and may reach professors of religion, and reports an alternative rendering of the last verse.

Clarke says flatly that there is no hope of the conversion of those who do not seek, renders the grief at the transgressors as being affected with anguish, and asks God to contend against the captors and bring his people out of bondage.

Ellicott holds the word rendered grieved far stronger than grief and intensified by a rare conjugation, so that it means being filled with loathing and sickened with disgust, quotes a modern hymn-writer to that effect, and renders the transgressors as the faithless or traitors; Keil and Delitzsch ground the prayer in the impossibility that God should let those faithful to his word succumb.

debates: Is the feeling of the hundred and fifty-eighth verse sorrow or revulsion? Gill and Henry both keep grief, Gill adding that it was less for the injuries done the speaker than for the ruin the transgressors brought on themselves, and Clarke renders it as being affected with anguish; Ellicott holds the Hebrew far stronger and intensified by a rare conjugation, so that the sense is being filled with loathing and sickened with disgust.

What is true from the beginning in the last verse? Gill and Henry both report an alternative rendering, that it is the sum or the beginning of God’s word which is truth; Henry adopts it and argues from it that the word did not acquire its validity by lapse of time, as human governments do, but was true at its beginning.
outliers: Henry cites a maxim of the civil law, that what at first wanted validity acquires it in the progress of time, and denies that God’s word holds by any such prescription.
Spurgeon calls the words for the speaker’s affliction picturesque, as portioning off a special spot of woe which he possesses as no one else ever did.
Henry marks that the plea is not to consider how the speaker keeps the precepts, since he was conscious of coming short, but how he loves them.
Henry allows that there were tender mercies enough in God to have saved even those from whom salvation is said to stand far off, had they not despised the riches of them.
themes: a request for attention rather than for speed
love pleaded where performance could not be
salvation receding as it is refused
disgust distinguished from sorrow at wrongdoing
a word denied any title by long usage

161.pericope_label: Princes have persecuted me without a cause: seven times a day do I praise thee

schools.summary: Spurgeon holds that a greater fear drove out the less and that princes appointed to protect the innocent shame themselves by assailing the righteous; Henry finds the aggravation in the law being on the persecutors’ side, notices that awe of the word and joy in it stand in consecutive verses and infers that reverence increases joy, and builds a doctrine of security on the promise that nothing shall offend those who love the law.

Gill takes the seven times for an indefinite number meaning very often, notes that the word is itself part of the armour by which the victory compared to spoil is won, and reads the hated lying as covering both common falsehood and false doctrine, superstition and idolatry.

Clarke applies the hatred of lying to captives who would not purchase release by making required confessions with an inward mental reservation, takes the spoil of the battlefield literally as the stripping of slain chiefs, and reports both a rabbinic reckoning of the seven daily praises and a tenth-century English homily prescribing a sevenfold rule of blessing, with the dry note that the sign of the cross was there thought sufficient without prayer; Wesley takes the number for an uncertain one.

Ellicott reads the persecution by princes as an indication of the psalm’s national character, allows that seven may be indefinite while noting its sacred associations and that the canonical hours were partly derived from this verse, and refuses to take the promise about stumbling as a statement of fact since the faithful plainly did stumble, offering to read it as a wish or as a description instead; Keil and Delitzsch sum the stanza as persecution in which the word remained his fear, his joy and his love.

debates: Are the seven daily praises to be counted? Gill, Henry and Wesley take the number for an indefinite one meaning very often; Ellicott reports that some do the same but observes that seven evidently carried a sacred association; Clarke allows the general sense yet reports a rabbinic authority who took it literally and distributed the seven around the two daily readings of the commandments, and both he and Ellicott hold that the canonical hours of the later church were partly derived from the verse.

Is it a fact that nothing offends those who love the law? Henry takes the promise as it stands and builds a doctrine of security on it, that no event of providence shall be either an invincible temptation or an intolerable affliction to such men; Ellicott declines the statement because it was not the fact that the faithful did not stumble, and offers to read the verse as a wish, great peace to the lovers of thy law and no stumbling-block to them, or as describing those who love the word and find no hindrance.
outliers: Clarke gives from a tenth-century English homily the sevenfold rule prescribed to every Christian man, at daybreak, mid-morning, midday, mid-afternoon, evening, bedtime and midnight if he should wake, and notes that the sign of the cross was there thought sufficient even without prayer.
Clarke applies the hatred of lying to men who might have satisfied their captors by a confession with inward mental reservation, and would not buy their release at that price.
Clarke takes the joy compared to great spoil of the plunder got by stripping the dead on a battlefield and taking the garments of slain chiefs.
Henry observes that awe of the word and joy in it stand in consecutive verses, and infers that the more reverence we have the more joy we shall find.
themes: one fear driving out another
power aggravated by having the law on its side
joy compared to plunder taken after a victory
a number read as a count and as a figure
a promise too large to be taken as a fact

169.pericope_label: Let my cry come near before thee, O Lord: I have gone astray like a lost sheep

schools.summary: Spurgeon personifies the prayer as a queen venturing into the royal presence to beg an audience, and draws the shape of the psalm’s ending, that nearness produces the lowest view of self so that the writer closes on his face begging to be sought like a lost sheep; Henry allows only one reason for wishing to live longer, that God may be praised in a world of conflict, notes that the man asking to be sought had himself been a shepherd, and ends where the psalm does, with a devout man living and dying repenting and praying.

Gill catches the fountain metaphor in the verb for uttering praise and reads the closing straying two ways, of a sheep wandering through inadvertence and corruption and of a man driven by persecution to wander from the courts of God.

Clarke calls the personified cry a fine image little heeded, made an intelligent being and sent to negotiate at the throne of grace, and compares the Greek epic in which prayers are the daughters of the chief god; he also distinguishes the lips that utter sounds attached to musical notes from the tongue that speaks intelligible words. Wesley leaves the last word with the text itself as the only ground of his hope.

Ellicott renders the uttering of praise as pouring forth a stream and the speaking of the following verse antiphonally, so that the tongue makes response to God’s word rather than speaks about it; Keil and Delitzsch pair the petitions for understanding and for deliverance, since a man persecuted for his faith needs that faith fortified as much as he needs release.

debates: What is the straying of the last verse? Gill offers two senses, a sheep wandering from the fold through inadvertence, the prevalence of corruption and the snares of the world, or a man driven by persecution to wander from the courts of God, which he says many interpreters prefer; Henry keeps the moral sense and observes that we are apt to wander like sheep and very unapt, once gone astray, to find the way again.
outliers: Clarke and Spurgeon independently take the opening verse for a personification, Clarke comparing the Greek epic in which prayers are made the daughters of the chief god and sent to negotiate, Spurgeon picturing the prayer as a queen venturing into the royal presence to beg an audience.
Clarke distinguishes the lips of one verse, which utter sounds attached to musical notes, from the tongue of the next, which speaks intelligible words.

Henry notes that the man who asks to be sought out had himself been a shepherd, and is asking God to seek him as he used to seek his own straying sheep; and he adds that to seek is to find, since God never seeks in vain.

Henry allows only one reason for a good man to wish to live longer, that he may praise God here, since we hope at death to go to a better world for that work, which is more agreeable for us though here there is more need of us.
themes: a prayer sent ahead as an envoy
singing distinguished from speaking
praise described as a stream rather than a duty
life desired for the sake of the praising
a psalm of obedience ending in confession
